content: have/has + the past participle makes the
PRESENT PERFECT — a past action with one
foot in the now.
I have finished.                    Press 1
She has left.                       Press 2
The participle is the past form's sibling:
- often the same:  say → said → said
- sometimes a third shape:
go → went → gone
take → took → taken
Learn each one as you meet it, never as
a table to memorize.
CONTRACTIONS: I have → I've,
she has → she's. Same words, fast speech.
Careful: she's = she is OR she has —
only the sentence tells you which.
She's happy. / She's gone home.
Many languages have a tense that is built
the same way but is simply their everyday
past. In English this one is special: it
ties a past action to the moment of now.
Two participles of go, two meanings:
BEEN = went there and came back.
I have been to the bank. (I'm back now)
GONE = went there and is still away.
He has gone to the bank. (still out)
"Have you ever been to...?" is how English
asks about a life experience.
In fast speech the helper contracts:
I haven't been.                     Press 1
You've never been?                  Press 2
He's gone out.                      Press 3
Haven't you gone yet?               Press 4
The perfect's little words, one job each:
ever    — at any time? (questions)
never   — at no time
already — sooner than expected
yet     — up to now (question/negative)
just    — a moment ago
Most sit in the middle, before the
participle: "I have never seen it."
But yet goes at the end:
"Have you finished yet?"
Your language places these small words
differently — watch where each one lands.
The time-word chooses the tense.
CLOSED TIME (it's over) → past simple:
yesterday, last week, ago, in 2019
I saw the film yesterday.           Press 1
She called twice last week.         Press 2
We spoke two days ago.              Press 3
OPEN TIME (still going) → present perfect:
today, this week, ever, so far
I have seen the film this week.     Press 4
She has called twice today.         Press 5
So far we have spoken twice.        Press 6

pronunciation_mappings.4: I have seen the film this week.
pronunciation_mappings.6: So far we have spoken twice.

content: FOR and SINCE measure the open time:
for + a length: "for ten years"
since + a start: "since Monday"
Same event, two tenses, two views:
"I lived here for years." (finished)
"I have lived here for years." (still)
Some languages use one past for both,
or use the perfect as the everyday past.
Here the time-word decides — read it first.
used to + verb = a habit in the past,
now over. The verb does not change.
I used to work here.                Press 1
She used to play every day.         Press 2
ASK and DENY with the do-engine (like
did) — used becomes use:
Did you use to live here?           Press 3
I didn't use to like it.            Press 4

pronunciation_mappings.2: She used to play every day.
pronunciation_mappings.3: Did you use to live here?
pronunciation_mappings.4: I didn't use to like it.

content: Do not confuse two look-alikes:
used to + verb = a past habit
I used to have long hair.        Press 1
(not now)
be used to + thing = it feels normal
I am used to the cold.           Press 2
(fine with it now)
Your first language may mark a past habit
in another way — your version shows how.

pronunciation_mappings.1: I used to have long hair.
pronunciation_mappings.2: I am used to the cold.

content: was / were + verb-ing = a scene that
was going on in the past.
She was sleeping.                   Press 1
We were carrying the boxes.         Press 2
It is the same -ing form you know for
'now', but with the past of be:
I / he / she / it  was
you / we / they     were
Two tenses tell the story together:
the long scene  = was/were + -ing
the quick event = past simple
I was carrying the box when I fell.    Press 1
scene: was carrying / event: fell
WHILE rides the long scene; WHEN rides
the quick event:
While she was cooking, the phone rang.
Your first language may build a scene and
a sudden event in another way — your
version shows how.

pronunciation_mappings.1: I was carrying the box when I fell.
